**A. The gate, with every known defect fixed (a).** Teacher v3 = 2-D stratified candidates (§5cs.87 fix) + full-lattice refinement (§5cs.88 fix) + random tie-breaking (§5cs.89 fix) + damage-only score + horizon 400. 497/500 states, 84/85 replays, ~75 min on 4 slots.

| | card | exact cell | 1-tile | mean dist |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| student v5lat s0 / s1 / s2 | 64.4 / 60.8 / 63.6 | **21.93 / 23.94 / 21.93** | 30.4 / 32.2 / 31.0 | 3.34 / 3.48 / 3.47 |
| teacher v1 (coarse, §5cs.87) | 100 | 0.00 | 1.01 | 12.475 |
| teacher v2 (refined, §5cs.88) | 100 | 0.00 | 2.01 | 12.562 |
| **teacher v3 (all fixes)** | 100 | **0.00** | 2.01 | **9.478** |

`GATE_cell_ge_student: false` on all three seeds, McNemar p ~1e-33 to ~1e-36 on cell. Card 100% is teacher-forcing by construction and carries no information.

**B. Why this one is not another artifact (a) -- the oracle check.** The obvious objection to every previous run was that the teacher could not *reach* the pro's cell. Measured directly from the per-candidate dump: for each state, the distance from the pro's placement to the **nearest candidate the teacher actually evaluated**.

| | mean | median |
|---|---|---|
| **oracle** (best candidate available to it) | **1.68 tiles** | 1.77 |
| **chosen** (what the score selected) | **13.54 tiles** | 14.84 |

**The near-pro placement was in the candidate set, was evaluated, and was rejected.** Reachability is not the constraint; the objective is. This is the measurement that separates "my search is broken" from "search disagrees with pros", and it lands on the second.

**C. What is and is not established.** Established (a): under a greedy one-shot rollout scored by tower damage dealt minus taken plus enemy units destroyed, over 400 ticks, **the best-scoring placement is systematically not the pro's placement** -- 9.5 tiles away on the full bench, against a student at 3.4. Not established (b): that *search* cannot beat the student. What failed is one specific objective. Three untested candidate causes, in the order I would test them: **no opponent model** (the rollout lets the opponent do nothing, so placements that would be punished look free); **horizon still short relative to an x-bow deck's payoff**, which accrues over tens of seconds of chip damage rather than one exchange; and **greedy single-placement scoring ignores sequencing**, while pro placements are often setup for the next card rather than locally optimal.

**D. A caveat on the oracle number (b).** It comes from the 18-state per-candidate dump taken before the tie-break fix, so the *chosen* column there (13.54) is the pre-fix teacher; the post-fix teacher is 9.478 on the full 497. The **oracle** column is a property of the candidate set, which the tie-break patch does not change, so it transfers -- but strictly the oracle for the v3 run is unmeasured, and a per-candidate dump on the fixed teacher would close that gap cheaply.

**E. Also still true and unchanged.** Exact-cell 0.00% is itself partly reachability-limited: an oracle of 1.68 tiles is far above the criterion's 0.3, so **no teacher with this candidate budget could score well on exact cell**, and the distance comparison is the honest one to read. The pre-registered criterion is not being revised to fit -- it is being reported as failed, with the note that the metric was more demanding than the search resolution ever supported.

**F. The recommendation.** Do not spend more compute widening the candidate set: B shows the objective, not the resolution, is what rejects pro-like placements. The next experiment is the **opponent model** -- re-run a subset with the opponent's real recorded plays continuing through the rollout window instead of an inert opponent, which is available for free from the replay and directly tests the first hypothesis in C. That is a one-shard, ~20-minute run and it should come before any further full-bench pass.


### §5cs.89 -- L66h (2026-09-07 13:0x-15:0x UTC): **the back-of-board bias is EXPLAINED and it was a tie-break artifact: ~40% of candidates tie at the maximum and "first wins" resolved every plateau to the lowest cy. Random tie-breaking cuts back-third placements from 7/18 to 2/18 -- but the teacher is still ~9 tiles from the pro against the student's 3.4, so it is a partial fix, not the answer**

**A. The measurement §5cs.88 F asked for (a), `scratchpad/gauntlet/L66/dump_cands.jsonl`, 18 states / 854 candidate evaluations.** Per-candidate scores, not just the winner:

| quantity | value |
|---|---|
| fraction of candidates tied at the maximum | median **0.39**, mean 0.40 |
| states where >50% of candidates tie at the max | 6 / 18 |
| score spread (max - min) within a state | median **213.1** |
| cy of the chosen winner | median **3.0** |
| lowest cy offered in that state | median **3.0** |

**The last two lines are the finding.** The landscape is *not* flat -- a spread of 213 means the score does discriminate -- but there is a large plateau at the top, and `try_cells` kept the FIRST maximum while candidates are generated in ascending cy. So in the median state the winner simply *was* the lowest-cy candidate on offer. **Explanation 2 of §5cs.88 D is confirmed: the 12.5-tile bias was an artifact of tie-break order, not of the objective.**

**B. The fix, and its limits (a).** Random tie-breaking among equal maxima (reservoir sampling, seeded), re-run on the same 18 states at two horizons:

| run | py median | in own back third | mean distance to pro |
|---|---|---|---|
| old, first-wins | 37.5 | 7/18 | 9.88 tiles |
| tie-break, horizon 120 | 32.0 | **2/18** | 9.62 tiles |
| tie-break, horizon 400 | 33.0 | **2/18** | **9.09 tiles** |
| pro | 42.0 | -- | -- |
| *student v5lat, full bench* | -- | -- | *3.34-3.48* |

Back-third placements fall from 39% to 11%, confirming the mechanism. **Distance barely moves: 9.88 -> 9.09 tiles, still ~2.7x the student's.** A longer horizon helps slightly and is kept.

**C. What B does NOT establish (b), and a caution against my own subset.** These 18 states are **not representative of the full bench**: the old run scored py median 37.5 and 7/18 back-third here, against 5.5 and 53% over all 497. The subset happens to be one where the artifact bit least, so **the improvement measured here is a lower bound on the fix and the residual 9-tile gap is an upper bound on nothing** -- 18 states is too few to size either. The full-bench run (tie-break, horizon 400, 4 slots, `nohup setsid` so it outlives the ssh session) is in flight and is the number that counts.

**D. Status (unchanged in substance).** The pre-registered S3 gate is still **not answered**. Two teacher defects are now found and fixed (a degenerate candidate sampler, §5cs.87; positional tie-breaking, here) and one hypothesis is dead (the unit-hp objection, §5cs.88 C). Whether searched targets agree with pros as often as the student does remains open, and **nothing measured so far licenses a claim either way** -- every teacher number to date has been dominated by a defect of mine rather than by search.

**E. A process trap worth keeping (a).** A deploy of `s3_teacher.py` silently did not apply: the remote command was `pkill ...; sleep 2; tar -xf - -C ~/cb && echo DEPLOYED`, and `DEPLOYED` printed while the file was unchanged (`grep -c dump_scores` = 0 remotely, 1 locally). The next run then failed on an unrecognised argument. **An echo that runs regardless of the copy is not a deploy check** -- verify the artifact on the far side, which is now done inline after every deploy. Related: an earlier `timeout 3000` on an ssh wrapper was shorter than the 90-minute job it was waiting on, and killed the wrapper while the remote work continued unattended; long remote runs now use `nohup setsid`.


### §5cs.88 -- L66g (2026-09-07 09:0x-13:0x UTC): **the sampler defect is FIXED (23 -> 85 distinct cells) and the gate still fails identically -- teacher exact-cell 0.00%, mean distance 12.56 tiles. The cause is a real back-of-board bias, and BOTH of my explanations for it are now contradicted or untested. The S3 gate is NOT answered and no "search disagrees with pros" claim is licensed by any of this**

**A. The refined run (a).** `--refine 2` re-searches the full lattice within +/-2 cells of the best coarse cell. 497/500 states, 84/85 replays, ~40 s/state/slot, ~2 h wall on 4 slots (2x the coarse run, as expected). It **fixed what §5cs.87 D diagnosed**: distinct teacher cells went from 23 across 497 states to **85**. The gate result did not move:

| | card | exact cell | 1-tile | mean dist |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| student v5lat s0 / s1 / s2 | 64.4 / 60.8 / 63.6 | **21.93 / 23.94 / 21.93** | 30.4 / 32.2 / 31.0 | 3.34 / 3.48 / 3.47 |
| teacher, coarse (§5cs.87) | 100.0 | 0.00 | 1.01 | 12.475 |
| **teacher, refined** | 100.0 | **0.00** | 2.01 | **12.562** |

`GATE_cell_ge_student: false` on all three seeds. Card is 100% by construction (teacher-forced) and is not evidence of anything.

**B. What is actually wrong (a).** The teacher places at the back of its own half: **median py 5.5 against the pros' 39.0**, and **264 of 497 (53%) in its own back third** (py < 16). Pro placements sit in a tight band (q1 35, q3 47) that the teacher rarely enters. A 12.5-tile mean distance on an 18x32 board is that bias, not noise.

**C. Explanation 1 -- CONTRADICTED (c).** I attributed it to the scoring function's unit term: `unit_swing` counted our units' *current* hitpoints, so placing a card adds its full hp to our side and placing it out of harm's way preserves that hp, while placing it into a fight spends it. The mechanism is real, so I wrote a v2 score that never counts our own units' hp as a gain -- damage only: enemy tower hp lost, plus enemy unit hp destroyed at 1/8, minus our tower hp lost. **On 68 states scored both ways, v2 median py is 5.5 with 38/68 in the back third, against v1's 28.5 and 32/68 on the same states.** Removing the term did not help and by that measure made it slightly worse. **The hypothesis is wrong.**

**D. Explanation 2 -- UNTESTED, and the data I have cannot decide it (b).** If the 120-tick (6 s) horizon leaves most candidates indistinguishable, the argmax is a tie-break, and `try_cells` keeps the FIRST maximum while coarse candidates are generated in ascending cy -- lowest cy is the back of the board. That would produce exactly this bias for both scoring functions, which fits. What I checked does **not** test it: best-scores vary richly *across states* (65 distinct values in 68, median 189), but the tie-break story is about spread *among candidates within* one state, which the output does not record. **Stating this as the cause would be a guess.**

**E. Status, plainly.** The pre-registered S3 gate is **not answered**. The teacher is not yet a valid instrument: one defect was found and fixed, a second is confirmed to exist and its cause is unknown. **Nothing here supports "searched targets do not agree with pros"** -- that claim would require a teacher whose placements are not dominated by an unexplained positional bias, and this one's are.

**F. The next measurement, specified.** Add a per-candidate score dump (state, cell, score) for ~10 states and read the within-state spread: if a large fraction of candidates tie at the maximum, D is the cause and the fixes are a longer horizon (so placements resolve) plus random tie-breaking; if scores are well separated and the maximum genuinely sits at the back, then the score is measuring something real that disagrees with pro doctrine and the horizon/objective needs rethinking rather than patching. That distinction is one short run and it should come before any further full-bench pass -- each of those is 2 hours.


### §5cs.87 -- L66f (2026-09-07 07:0x-09:0x UTC): **the S3 search teacher is built and runs the full bench (497/500 states, 46 min on 4 VM slots). Its first gate run is INVALID and must not be read as a result: with 24 near-fixed candidates the exact-cell criterion was unreachable by construction, so the 0.0% measures my sampler, not search. Refined re-run in flight**

**A. What was built (a).** `pipeline/s3_teacher.py`. For each benchmark state it re-drives the replay to the branch tick, places a candidate in `libg`, rolls forward `--horizon` ticks, and scores tower damage dealt minus taken plus a 1/8-weight unit-hitpoint term. Three deliberate constraints so the gate stays a test of search: the **card is teacher-forced** to the pro's slot exactly as `s3_bench.predict` reads the student's cell head; candidates are generated **on the model's own 36x64 lattice** and converted to engine coordinates from there (a continuously-placing teacher would beat a quantised student on sub-cell precision alone); and the score uses **no learned value**, which would otherwise import the student's biases into its own examiner.

**B. Student baseline on these 500 states (a), the bar the teacher must clear.** `s1_icebow_v5lat_s{0,1,2}` via `s3_bench predict`:

| seed | card | exact cell | 1-tile | mean dist (tiles) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| s0 | 64.39 | 21.93 | 30.38 | 3.34 |
| s1 | 60.76 | 23.94 | 32.19 | 3.48 |
| s2 | 63.58 | 21.93 | 30.99 | 3.47 |

**C. Cost, measured (a).** 497 of 500 states produced a target (99.4%; the 3 losses are ability plays or episodes already terminal at the branch tick), 84 of 85 replays, **~22 s/state per slot and ~46 min wall on 4 slots** at 24 candidates and horizon 120. Each candidate is a full re-drive to the branch tick because the engine protocol has no snapshot op, and that is the entire cost.

**D. THE GATE RUN IS INVALID -- do not read its numbers (c).** It reported teacher exact-cell **0.00%** against the student's 21.9-23.9, mean distance **12.475 tiles**, and `GATE_cell_ge_student: false` on all three seeds with McNemar p ~1e-33. None of that is evidence about search, because of a defect in my candidate generation:

- the teacher used **23 distinct cells across all 497 states** -- the coarse 4x6 lattice is nearly state-independent, since the legal-region bounding box barely changes;
- the criterion is agreement within **0.3 tiles** on a 36x64 lattice of 2,304 cells. A fixed 24-cell menu **cannot land within 0.3 tiles of an arbitrary pro placement except by coincidence**, so 0.0% was determined by the design before the engine ran.

**The failure was guaranteed by construction and the run measures my sampler, not the teacher.** Recorded here rather than quietly re-run, because a "search targets disagree with pros" headline drawn from this would have been exactly the kind of confident wrong conclusion this journal exists to catch. It also sits alongside the earlier candidate bug in the same file (a row-major stride collapsing every proposal onto cx=0) -- **twice now, the sampler rather than the search decided the answer.**

**E. A second signal, real but unmeasured (b).** Teacher `py` median **5.5** against pro median **39.0**: the search overwhelmingly chose the back of its own half. That is consistent with the scoring function rewarding *safety* -- a placement far from the action takes no tower damage and scores ~0, which beats a placement that trades unfavourably. Whether that is the scoring function's fault or a genuine property of one-shot greedy placement is **not established** and needs its own test once D is fixed. It is the next thing to look at if the refined run still disagrees with pros.

**F. The fix now running.** `--refine R` adds a stage B: after the coarse pass, re-search every legal cell within +/-R cells of the best coarse cell at full lattice resolution (R=2 gives 24 coarse + up to 24 fine evaluations, roughly 2x cost). This makes the pre-registered criterion **reachable**, which is the precondition for the gate meaning anything. The pre-registered criterion itself is unchanged -- it was fixed before the teacher existed and is not being tuned to the result.


### §5cs.86 -- L66e (2026-09-07 06:3x-07:0x UTC): **VERDICT: anonymous video mining is NOT worth continuing. Best case +0.3 to +0.5 pp for days of work and ~46 h of throttled downloading, with an untested discount on top. Engine slots scale 2.68x at 4 slots (3,400 matches/hour), so S3 is now the cheap path and mining is the expensive one**

**A. The owner's ruling and the question it left.** "I'm not risking my account" -- so the cookie route is closed, and the question is whether *anonymous* mining is worth continuing. This is that verdict.

**B. What mining would return (b, arithmetic on measured inputs).** Hit rate 1/20 = 5.0% [0.9-23.6%] (§5cs.85 E) over 441.6 channel hours, at 170 s of battle per match (§5cs.80 C):

| icebow supply | matches | doublings | gain at 1.50 pp/doubling |
|---|---|---|---|
| point estimate, 22 h | 259-466 | 0.21-0.36 | **+0.32 to +0.54 pp** |
| optimistic bound, 104 h | 1,224-2,202 | 0.80-1.23 | +1.21 to +1.84 pp |

**C. What it would cost (a for the rate, b for the extrapolation).** Anonymous fetching is now rate-limited by bot detection after ~11 videos at 4-way parallelism. Serial fetching may evade it -- **untested** -- but at the measured ~2 min per 180 s slice, classifying all 1,382 videos is **~46 hours of wall clock** before a single frame is mined, then full downloads of the ~70 hits, then the mining pipeline itself (board->tile homography, hand and elixir reading, IDM labelling, the precision/recall gate) which is days of work and entirely unbuilt.

**D. The discount nobody has measured (b).** Every number above assumes a mined replay is worth as much as a sandbox-driven one. It almost certainly is not: the +1.50 pp/doubling slope was fitted on replays with exact unit state, while a mined replay carries detector noise in **both the observation and the label**. The true return is the table in B times an unknown factor <= 1.

**E. VERDICT: stop.** Half a percentage point, conditional on an untested download workaround, an unbuilt pipeline, and an unmeasured quality discount -- against S3, where §5cs.85 just moved compute from 347 local hours per 100k matches to **69 VM-hours (~$27)**, and where the engine produces exact-state data without a rate limiter or a terms-of-service question. Mining is not refuted as an idea; it is simply the worse use of the same nights. The instruments (`deckid.py`, `profile.py`, `sweep.sh`) are committed and calibrated, so if the channel's icebow fraction is ever worth re-testing, the cost is one command, not a rebuild.

**F. Slot scaling, measured (a).** Four slots in one AVD, same 24 tags each, all four returning 17 files:

| slots | per-slot median | aggregate | speedup | efficiency |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2.48 s | 1,267 matches/h | 1.00x | 100% |
| 4 | 3.58-3.67 s | **3,400 matches/h** | **2.68x** | 67% |

Sub-linear, as expected, and the likely reason is that the emulator was launched with `-cores 4` (`worker.py:147-155`) on an 8-vCPU host -- so four slots saturate the guest's four cores. **Untested:** whether relaunching the AVD with `-cores 8` recovers the rest. 3,400 matches/hour is already ~12x the local box, so this is not the bottleneck for anything S3 needs next.


### §5cs.85 -- L66d (2026-09-07 05:4x-06:3x UTC): **the VM drives replays 5.0x faster than this box on identical work -- 2.48 s/match vs 12.52 s -- so S3 compute is roughly an order of magnitude cheaper than §5cs.55 assumed. Separately, YouTube's bot detection stopped the sweep at 11/100, and the icebow hit rate is now 1/20**

**A. Engine throughput, apples to apples (a).** Same 24 tags, same `--record-every 20 --record-plays --determinism-every 10`, same 17 that drive successfully (the other 7 are the known evo-E-barb class), and **both sides produced 17 files with a median of 240 recorded frames** -- verified, because identical output is what makes the timings comparable.

| | s/match median | batch wall | matches/hour/slot |
|---|---|---|---|
| this box (Windows, WHPX, 64% CPU) | **12.52** | 254 s | 288 |
| clashbot-s3 (Linux, KVM, 1 slot) | **2.48** | 48.3 s | 1,452 |

**5.0x.** On cores that benchmark *slower* (0.79x integer, 0.56x float, §5cs.80 E). Contention is not the explanation: the local box read **12.52 s/match at 64% CPU now**, which is *worse* than the 10.71 s median measured while training was saturating it, so the local figure is not depressed by load. The remaining candidate is the hypervisor -- Windows WHPX versus Linux KVM for Android emulation -- which is untested as a cause and would need a same-host A/B to prove.

**B. A near-miss worth recording (c).** The first VM run reported **1.43 s/match** and I nearly had a 7.5x headline. It was measuring different work: I had omitted the recording flags, so the drives produced `frames: 0`. The check that caught it was reading the output files rather than the timing line -- `frames: 0` vs the local corpus's 240. **A throughput number is meaningless until you confirm both sides produced the same artifact**, which is the §7 "never compare two instruments" rule wearing a new hat.

**C. What this does to S3 sizing (b, arithmetic on a measured rate).** At 2.48 s/match on a single slot, 100,000 driven matches costs **69 VM-hours (~$27)**; the sandbox supports up to 8 slots per AVD, and if slots scale even sub-linearly the same work is single-digit dollars. Against the §5cs.55 estimate of ~400 slot-hours, **compute has stopped being the S3 constraint** -- on the local box that same 100k would be 347 hours. Multi-slot scaling is **untested** and is the next thing to measure; nothing here says 8 slots give 8x.

**D. The sweep was stopped by YouTube, not by us (a).** Of 100 videos, **11 downloaded and 88 failed** with `Sign in to confirm you're not a bot`, plus 2 timeouts. Four-way parallel fetching tripped bot detection partway through. The documented workaround is `--cookies-from-browser`, i.e. authenticating as the owner's Google account -- which is a **materially different risk from anonymous fetching**: it attaches the activity to a personal account and makes account-level enforcement possible. The owner acknowledged the ToS point when the operation was anonymous; this is a new fact, so it goes back to them rather than being assumed covered. The untested cheaper option is simply to fetch slowly and serially.

**E. Hit rate, updated (a).** The 10 sweep videos that did download all scored **0.487-0.584**, i.e. none reach the 0.60 threshold. Combined with the paired pilot set: **1 icebow in 20 videos = 5.0%**, Wilson 95% CI **0.9-23.6%**. Against 441.6 channel hours that is **22 h of icebow footage, band 4-104 h**, versus the **78-139 h** one corpus doubling needs (§5cs.80 C). The point estimate is now well short and the upper bound barely reaches the requirement. **The direction of evidence has moved against video mining as a scaling lever** -- 20 videos is still a small sample, but it is no longer consistent with "dozens if not hundreds" of icebow videos on this channel.


### §5cs.84 -- L66c (2026-09-07 05:0x-05:3x UTC): **FIRST ENGINE SLOT RUNNING ON LINUX. `{"ready": true, "mode": "serve-direct", "slot": 0, "port": 37031}` on clashbot-s3 in 14.2 s. The port is confirmed end to end -- `libg.so` loads and serves inside a nested-KVM AVD on a GCP VM**

**A. The milestone (a).** `bash scripts/start_direct_service.sh --serial emulator-5554 --port 37031 --slot 0` returns the same JSON contract as the PowerShell original: `{"ready": true, "mode": "serve-direct", "slot": 0, "port": 37031, "serial": "emulator-5554", "remote_root": "/data/local/tmp/cr-native-direct-0", "guest_pids": [2738], "state": {...}}`. Readiness required a successful `ping` **and** a `status` round trip over the adb-forwarded socket, so the engine is not merely launched, it is answering.

**B. The port needed no repair (a).** Everything §5cs.81 tested green in isolation held in the real run: the triple-nested launch string, the adb forward, `push_verified`'s sha256 skip, the `unzip`-instead-of-`tar` asset extraction, the `ps` matcher. The first attempt already got as far as `{"schema_version":1,"stage":"jni_on_load","event":"after_system_load","ok":true}` -- **the real `libg.so` loaded natively in the guest** -- before failing for an unrelated reason (C). No line of the translated script was wrong.

**C. NEW TRAP: the start script does not install the game (a).** First attempt died at `JniHost.createPackageContext` with `PackageManager$NameNotFoundException: Application package com.supercell.clashroyale not found`. The APKs are *pushed* to `/data/local/tmp/...` by the start script but **installing them is a separate step that lives in `native_core/worker.py:184-194`** (`adb install-multiple -r -t`, base.apk sorted first, all five splits), not in `start_direct_service.ps1`. On the Windows box that install happened once at bootstrap and has persisted in the AVD ever since, which is exactly why it is invisible until a fresh AVD. `adb install-multiple` on the VM: **Success in 8.2 s**. Anyone standing up a new AVD hits this, and the error message names a package rather than a missing step, so it does not point at its own cause.

**D. Timings, and what they say about slot cost (a).** First start **4m 3s**, second start **14.2 s**. The difference is `push_verified`: 75 MB of `.so` plus `base.apk` are pushed and sha256-verified once, then skipped on every later start because the guest hashes already match -- so the steady-state cost of (re)starting a slot is ~14 s, not 4 minutes, and that is what matters for a worker pool that restarts slots. The 4-minute figure is a one-off per AVD.

**E. What is still unmeasured (b).** Engine THROUGHPUT -- replay-drives per hour against the local box's 11.24 s/match median (§5cs.78 E) -- needs the replay corpus on the VM and has not been run. That is the number that sizes S3 (how many VM-hours the ~400 slot-hour estimate really costs), and it is the next measurement. Note the VM's single core is 0.79x/0.56x of a local core (§5cs.80 E), so a naive expectation is ~14-20 s/match per slot; whether 8 uncontended cores beat one contended Windows box is exactly the open question.


### §5cs.83 -- L66b (2026-09-07 04:0x-04:4x UTC): **the deck identifier is CALIBRATED and found its first true positive -- `NYAWcJcGU3E` scores 0.730, above all three known-icebow controls, with all eight cards at 0.73-0.83. Threshold 0.60 separates two populations with a 0.06 gap. Hit rate 1/9, whose 95% band (2-43%) brackets the answer, so a 100-video sweep is running**

**A. Separation, at the slice length §5cs.82 E established (a), `profile180*.json`.**

| population | file | worst_icebow (min over the 8 cards of that card's max score) |
|---|---|---|
| known icebow | ctrl_hunter1_180s | 0.625 |
| known icebow | ctrl_hunter2_180s | 0.670 |
| known icebow | ctrl_hunter3_180s | 0.687 |
| **discovered icebow** | **NYAWcJcGU3E** | **0.730** |
| other decks (8 channel videos) | -- | 0.500, 0.509, 0.517, 0.530, 0.534, 0.548, 0.565, 0.500 |

Threshold **0.60**: min positive 0.625, max negative 0.565, gap 0.060. `NYAWcJcGU3E`'s per-card profile is unambiguous -- tornado 0.730, tesla 0.759, ice_wizard 0.766, x_bow 0.778, rocket 0.804, knight 0.752, the_log 0.829, skeletons 0.765 -- eight cards, none weak. Against it the strongest non-icebow card reaches 0.779, so even its *worst* deck member is within 0.05 of the best false match; the discriminator is that all eight clear 0.73 at once, which no other deck's profile does.

**B. It confirms the retraction rather than softening it (c -> a).** `NYAWcJcGU3E` is the exact video whose hand strip I flagged by eye (tornado, rocket, greyed x-bow) and which the discarded 20-second pilot scored 0.545 and called negative. Same video, same instrument, longer slice: **0.545 -> 0.730**. The pilot did not merely lack power; it inverted a positive. Had the sweep been built on it, the channel would have been written off as having no icebow at all.

**C. The number that decides the plan is still uncertain (a, and honestly so).** Hit rate **1 of 9 = 11.1%**, Wilson 95% CI **2.0% - 43.5%**. Against 441.6 channel hours that is **49 h of icebow footage, band 9-192 h** -- and one corpus doubling needs 78-139 h (§5cs.80 C). **The point estimate is SHORT of a doubling and the band straddles it**, so the honest statement is that nine videos cannot answer this. Sampling 100 tightens the rate to about +/-6 pp, which is enough to separate "not worth it" from "one doubling" -- that sweep is running (`sweep.sh`, 4-way parallel, ~21 MB per video).

**D. Cost model, now measured not estimated (a).** 180 s at <=720p averages **21 MB** and about 2 min of wall clock per video serially, 4-way parallel in the sweep; profiling is ~26 s per video single-core. Stage 1 over all 1,382 videos is therefore ~29 GB and, at 4-way parallelism, roughly 12 hours -- or about 3 hours at 16-way. Stage 2 (full download of the hits only) is ~1.4 GB per hit-hour.

**E. Unchanged and still the largest unknown (b).** Everything above is about how much icebow footage EXISTS. What a mined replay is worth relative to a sandbox-driven one is still unmeasured, and the +1.50 pp/doubling slope was fitted entirely on engine-driven data with exact unit state. A mined corpus carries detector noise in both the observation and the label. **Nothing here licenses assuming they are interchangeable**, and the cheapest way to find out is to mine one hit-video and compare a model trained with it against one trained without.


### §5cs.82 -- L66 (2026-09-07 02:4x-04:0x UTC): **the runtime is on the VM (libg.so hash matches byte-for-byte) and the channel holds 441.6 hours across 1,382 videos. A deck identifier was built in four passes, three of which were wrong; the pilot that used it is DISCARDED because 20-second clips cannot show an 8-card deck -- measured on known-icebow footage, not argued**

**A. Owner rulings.** Q2 granted (runtime may be copied to the VM). Q1 answered with a task: identify which of HunterCR's videos are icebow by inspecting frames, verify card-by-card that all eight are present, and see how much footage that yields.

**B. Runtime is on clashbot-s3 (a).** 1.1 GB transferred over ssh (`tar | ssh tar -x`), 5 APKs + 14 `.so` + 383 DataTables. **`libg.so` sha256 `<libg/sampler hash, local>` on both ends** -- identical to the hash `bindings/runtime-manifest.json` pins, so the version freeze survived the move. Nothing under any `*/data/` path was included.

**C. Channel inventory (a), metadata only, no video fetched.** `yt-dlp --flat-playlist`: **1,382 videos, 441.6 hours, median 17.0 min**, 1,379 of them over 10 minutes. So the raw supply comfortably exceeds the 78-139 video-hours that §5cs.80 measured as one corpus doubling -- *if* enough of it is icebow, which is the open question.

**D. The deck identifier (a), `scratchpad/gauntlet/L66/deckid.py` + `profile.py`.** Read the HAND, not the board: the four hand slots and the "Next" slot sit at fixed fractions of a full-screen portrait capture, the art is large and unoccluded, and a cycling deck shows all eight cards over enough frames. Matching is NCC against `icebow/templates/cards/` (2,174 crops, 110 cards, 64x80, captured from our own screen), evo folded to base keys. Slot boxes were read off a labelled coordinate grid on a real frame, not guessed. **It took four passes and the first three were wrong:**

1. **Whole-crop dot product.** Compared a slot box (card + border + elixir badge) against templates that are *tighter* crops of just the art. Calibration on known-icebow footage: non-icebow p90 0.635-0.691 sat **above** the icebow median 0.51-0.567 -- i.e. it ranked wrong cards higher than right ones. Fixed by sliding the template inside the slot at multiple scales (x_bow 0.80, rocket 0.82, tornado 0.75, tesla 0.73 after the fix).
2. **Evo names.** The deck is `tesla_evo`/`knight_evo`, the matcher reads `tesla`/`knight` off the same art. Folded to base keys -- deck identity does not depend on which two slots are evolved.
3. **Kept only each slot's top-2.** A card that was never any slot's argmax got no score and defaulted to 0.000, which made a **known-icebow video read `worst_icebow = 0.000`**, indistinguishable from any other deck. The per-card scores were being computed and thrown away. Fixed by returning the full vector (`slot_card_scores`).

The surviving readout is per-video, not per-slot: for each of the eight icebow cards take its max score over all slots and frames; the verdict is the **worst** of those eight. A real icebow deck's weakest member still beats every card it does not play; another deck can share two or three commodity cards (log, rocket, skeletons) but not eight.

**E. THE PILOT IS DISCARDED (c) -- and this is the load-bearing finding.** Twelve videos sampled at random from the channel, 20-second clips, all twelve scored `worst_icebow` 0.483-0.545 against known-icebow footage at 0.623-0.634 -- an apparently clean 0/12. **It is uninformative.** A controlled test on footage known to be icebow, cut the same way the pilot was:

| footage | slice | frames sampled | worst_icebow |
|---|---|---|---|
| known icebow (HunterCR_1) | 20 s | 6 | **0.558** |
| known icebow (HunterCR_1) | 180 s | 6 | **0.625** |
| known icebow (HunterCR_1) | 180 s | 20 | **0.625** |

**Slice LENGTH decides it, frame count does not** (0.625 either way). Twenty seconds is two or three hands; an eight-card deck has not cycled, so several cards never enter the hand and the minimum-over-eight collapses. Every pilot clip was measured in the regime where genuine icebow reads ~0.56. The eyeball check agreed before the numbers did: the hand strip of `NYAWcJcGU3E` (the highest "negative" at 0.545) shows tornado, rocket and a greyed x-bow. **No conclusion about the channel's icebow fraction survives, in either direction.** Re-running the same twelve at 180 s, paired.

**F. What the re-run costs, and the shape of the real job (b).** One match (~180 s) at <=720p is ~30 MB, so classifying all 1,382 videos costs ~40 GB and one pass of downloads; only the videos that pass would then be fetched in full. That is a two-stage design and the stage-1 slice must be at least one match long -- which is exactly what E establishes and what a 20-second stage 1 would have got wrong at scale.

**G. Standing caveat, unchanged by any of this (b).** Even a large icebow haul buys corpus doublings at +1.50 pp each (§5cs.78), and video-mined data is not engine-quality: the scaling slope was measured on replays driven through the sandbox with exact unit state, while mined data would carry detector noise in both observation and label. **The slope does not transfer to noisier data by assumption**, and nothing measured so far says what a mined replay is worth relative to a driven one.


### §5cs.81 -- L65c (2026-09-07 02:0x-02:3x UTC): **the sandbox's Linux port is written and its two riskiest lines are TESTED GREEN on the VM, using zero game binaries. A tar assumption of mine was load-bearing and is now verified rather than asserted; a patch of mine was broken and was caught by reading it back**

**A. What was built.** `scratchpad/gauntlet/L65/port/` -- `start_direct_service.sh` (the 175-line PowerShell launcher), `stop_direct_service.sh` (25), `worker_linux.patch.py` (four platform branches in `native_core/worker.py`, idempotent, `--check` mode), `runtime.env.sh.example`. The port lives in scratchpad because the sandbox sits under `research/ext/`, which this project never commits; the patch script applies it to the working tree on demand. **Not applied yet** -- the Windows path is what drives corpora today and there is no reason to touch it before the runtime question is settled.

**B. The launch nesting is green (a), `scratchpad/gauntlet/L65/port/_port_probe.sh` run on clashbot-s3.** The survey named this as the trap: `nohup sh -c "cd ... && exec env CLASSPATH=... app_process ..." >log 2>&1 </dev/null &`, handed to `adb shell` as one argument and re-parsed by the guest shell, fails as a service that starts and instantly exits with no diagnostic but an in-guest log. Tested with `env` and `sleep` standing in for `app_process`, on the live AVD:

| check | result |
|---|---|
| `CLASSPATH` arrives intact in the guest | yes, both paths, `:`-joined |
| `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` arrives intact | yes |
| backgrounded process survives the adb session closing | yes |
| `service_pids()` awk matcher finds it by class + root + subcommand | yes, pid 2281 |
| `adb forward tcp:37031` round trip | established, listed |
| `push` + host/guest sha256 agreement (`push_verified`) | yes |

So the real launch differs from the tested one only in which binary is exec'd.

**C. A load-bearing assumption of mine, verified not asserted (a).** The `.ps1` runs `tar.exe -xf <asset-pack>.apk` (`start_direct_service.ps1:110`). Windows' `tar.exe` is bsdtar/libarchive, which reads zip archives -- and an APK is a zip. I claimed GNU tar cannot, and replaced that one call with `unzip`. Tested on the VM against a real zip: **GNU tar 1.34 fails, `unzip` works.** The claim holds, and a mechanical `.ps1 -> .sh` transliteration would have died at exactly that line with "This does not look like a tar archive". This trap is not in the portability survey.

**D. My own patch was broken, caught by reading it back (c).** The first draft of edit 3 wrapped the existing `command = [...]` in `if os.name == "nt":` and stopped -- which leaves `command` **undefined on Linux**, the exact platform the patch exists for. `--check` reported "4 anchors matched" and told me nothing about it, because an anchor matching is not the same as a replacement being correct. Fixed by replacing the whole block including both branches. **The general lesson, which is the same one as §5cs.80 D: a check that only confirms the thing you already believed is not a test.**

**E. What is still unmeasured and why (b).** Engine throughput per VM slot -- replay-drives per hour against the local box's 11.24 s/match median -- cannot be measured without the game runtime, which is behind the owner's ruling in §5cs.80 H. Everything cheaper than that ruling has now been done: nested KVM (§5cs.80 G-RESULT, 35 s boot), the adb mechanics, the launch quoting, the asset-extraction path. What remains is `sdkmanager`/`avdmanager` bootstrap (deferrable convenience) and the first real engine start.


### §5cs.80 -- L65 (2026-09-07 01:3x-02:2x UTC): **the HunterCR footage is genuinely mineable -- and holds ~19-34 matches, worth +0.03 pp on the measured scaling curve. The S3 VM is up with nested virt live, and the sandbox is NOT Windows-locked: ~200 lines of PowerShell orchestration is the whole port**

**A. Owner ruling and how it was tested.** The owner supplied three HunterCR recordings and ruled: *"if you decide those videos are good, proceed with the mining first"*, plus *"you can run the VM while the mining runs"*. The condition is doing real work here, so both halves of "good" were measured.

**B. Framing: good, and my §5cs.79 objection does NOT apply (a).** 888x1920 and 592x1280 **portrait full-screen phone capture**, 60 fps, fixed camera, whole board in frame, **card hand + next-card + elixir bar visible**, tower HP and match clock visible, and the game prints its own **deploy label at the placement ring** ("Ice Wizard lvl 16", "Knight lvl 15", "Tesla lvl 15") -- free card-identity ground truth. Every one of the three things `bridgeblock.mp4` lacked is present. **In-battle fraction 96.1 / 95.8 / 96.2 %** (`scratchpad/gauntlet/L65/survey.json`): the recordings are cut to remove menus, so 95.8 of the 96.7 minutes are live battle.

**C. Volume: the number that decides it (a), `scratchpad/gauntlet/L65/matchcount.json`.** **19 matches (lower bound), ~34 (upper)**, in 96.7 minutes -- about 170 s of battle per match. Against the 1,638-replay icebow corpus that is **+1.2 % to +2.1 %, i.e. 0.017-0.030 doublings, i.e. +0.025 to +0.044 pp** at the measured 1.50 pp/doubling (§5cs.78). **One corpus doubling would take 78-139 hours of this footage.** The footage is good and there is ~50-80x too little of it to move the curve.

**D. Two counting errors, both mine, both caught (c).** (1) `_survey.py` counted matches as runs of in-battle frames separated by a >= 20 s menu gap and returned **1 match per file** -- wrong, because these recordings cut the menus out; all 811 s of HunterCR_1 merged into one "match". The opponent-name HUD crop disproved it directly: der Namenlose -> AmiR -> Kun|YiNian -> KNE LANGEXX inside that one file. (2) The replacement counted name-crop CHANGES but thresholded the diff at 0.12 against the previous sample, while real name changes measure only ~0.09 (`jitter_p99`) -- so it also returned 1. Fixed by comparing against the block's reference mask (within-match diff is exactly 0.000) with a 0.02 threshold and a 2-sample persistence rule. **The lesson is the same one twice: a detector whose threshold was never calibrated against its own measured noise is not an instrument.** The final count is still a LOWER bound -- consecutive matches against the same opponent read as one, and four blocks are exactly double-length (336-346 s vs the modal 170 s), which is what that looks like.

**E. The VM is up and nested virt is real (a).** Owner hit `CPUS_ALL_REGIONS` = 12 globally on the 16-vCPU request -- **a retraction: I read the regional `N2_CPUS` = 200 and told them no quota request was needed; the binding cap was the global one.** `n2-standard-8` fits under it and costs nothing in total compute (the $300 buys ~6,100 core-hours either way; fewer cores only stretches wall-clock). `clashbot-s3` is RUNNING at 34.173.75.16: ssh with the project key works, **8 vCPU, 31 GB RAM, `/dev/kvm` present, 16 `vmx` flags, 192 GB free, Ubuntu 22.04.5**. Single-core speed vs this box: **0.79x integer, 0.56x float** (`_cpubench.py`, identical source both sides) -- so a VM core is roughly two-thirds of a local core and the 8 of them are uncontended, against a local box that has been at 90-100 % all night.

**F. The sandbox is portable (a), `scratchpad/gauntlet/L65/sandbox_portability.md`, 177 lines with file:line citations.** It runs the real game's `libg.so` headless inside a stock AOSP Android 31 x86_64 AVD -- host CPU executes the game code natively, the emulator supplies only the Android userland. "Engine slot 37031" = an `adb forward`-ed TCP port to an `app_process ... royale.nativehost.JniHost serve-direct` process in the guest. **Nothing in the execution path is a Windows binary** (`libg.so` and `libnative_core_probe.so` are ELF64, `lifecycle-probe.jar` is dexed); `pyproject.toml` declares no dependencies at all. The entire Windows surface is orchestration: `worker.py:57-58` shelling to `powershell.exe`, `.exe` suffixes at `:76,:80`, and `start_direct_service.ps1` (175 lines) + `stop_direct_service.ps1` (25). **Port cost: half a day to a day**, and the trap is named in advance -- the triple-nested quoting at `start_direct_service.ps1:145-146`, which fails as a service that starts and instantly exits with no diagnostic but an in-guest `service.log`.

**G. The test now running, and why this one first (b -> a when it lands).** Nested KVM was the survey's one untested unknown: on Linux `-accel on` means KVM, and this host is itself a VM, so it is KVM inside a guest. `scratchpad/gauntlet/L65/vm_kvm_test.sh` boots a stock AOSP AVD with `worker.py:147-155`'s exact flags and times it. **It needs zero game binaries**, so it can kill the cloud plan before anyone moves 1.15 GB or rules on whether that move is allowed.

**G-RESULT (a), `~/kvm_test.json` on clashbot-s3.** The nested-KVM unknown is settled: the stock AOSP 31 x86_64 AVD booted headless with `worker.py`'s exact flags in **35 seconds** (`boot_completed=1`), `kvm-ok` reports acceleration usable, `adb root` succeeds (uid=0, which the sandbox requires and is why Google Play images are rejected), and the whole Android SDK + system image pulled in 53 s. That is bare-metal-class boot time, not the degraded nested-virt case the survey warned about. **The cloud plan survives its riskiest test, and it was tested with zero game binaries.** What this does NOT establish: emulator boot is not engine throughput -- how many replay-drives per hour a VM slot sustains is unmeasured and needs the runtime, i.e. it is behind the question in H.

**H. The blocker that is the owner's to decide, not mine.** The runtime bundle (964 MB of APKs + 75 MB of `.so` + 4.6 MB of DataTables) is **explicitly non-redistributable** -- the sandbox repo ships none of it and its MIT licence excludes the game binaries. Copying files the owner obtained legally onto a cloud VM the owner controls is plausibly fine and is still their call, not a default I should take on their behalf. Posted with the footage question.


### §5cs.79 -- L64v (2026-09-07 01:4x-02:1x UTC): **the detector does NOT collapse on third-party video (2.05 dets/frame at conf 0.59 vs 3.72 at 0.71 on our own capture) -- but the clip we hold is an EDITED highlight reel with a panning camera, no hand and no elixir bar, so it cannot be mined at any detector quality. Two of my own premises contradicted. Recommendation: drop video mining, go to S3**

**A. What was measured (a), `scratchpad/gauntlet/L64/idm/transfer_probe.json`, 60 frames per arm, conf 0.25, imgsz 960, 46-card whitelist.**

| arm | dets/frame | whitelist/frame | frames with any det | mean conf |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A our own session `20260815_222309` | 3.72 | 3.10 | 54/60 | 0.712 |
| B `bridgeblock.mp4` native 640x360 | 2.05 | 1.35 | 47/60 | 0.590 |
| C B upscaled to height 1198 | 1.97 | 1.32 | 48/60 | 0.602 |

The detector fires on third-party footage at roughly half the rate and 0.12 lower mean confidence, with a coherent class mix (skeletons, knight, balloon, tesla, elixir_golemite, graveyard) rather than the scatter a detector reading noise would produce. **The collapse hypothesis is not supported.** What this can NOT say: the two clips show different decks and different unit densities, so dets/frame is not a recall comparison -- only a labelled measurement is.

**B. CONTRADICTED: my own description of the video (c).** The probe's premise was "the phone screen occupies maybe 200x360 px of a landscape frame, ~10x fewer arena pixels". Looking at the frames (`frame_mid.png`, `frames_4up.png`): `bridgeblock.mp4` is an edited highlight clip -- a **panning, zooming crop of part of the arena**, with overlaid card-name captions ("Mini P.E.K.K.A lvl 1", "Skeletons"), colour-tint effects, **no card hand and no elixir bar in frame**, and never the whole board. The arena is at HIGHER magnification than our own capture, which is why detections held up.

**C. CONTRADICTED: arm C tested nothing (c).** YOLO letterboxes to imgsz=960 on the longest side, so 640x360 and its 2129x1198 upscale reach the model as the same 960x540 tensor. C == B by construction (1.97 vs 2.05 is the frame-sampling difference), and the resolution-vs-domain question it was built to answer is still open. A real resolution arm must crop the arena region first. Both corrections are now written into the probe's docstring so the file cannot mislead a later loop.

**D. The finding that actually decides the S2 item (a).** Detector quality was never the binding constraint on this clip. IDM mining needs, per frame: a fixed board->pixel mapping (the camera must not pan or zoom), the hand (which card was played), and the elixir bar (whether a play was affordable). This clip has none of the three. **Mining requires unedited full-screen gameplay recordings**, which is a sourcing problem, not a modelling one, and the only unedited footage we hold is our own three sessions (597 MB, which already carry `events.jsonl` ground truth and so are the right target for the labelled precision/recall measurement, not for corpus growth).

**E. Recommendation: stop here and go to S3 (b -- a judgement, with the numbers behind it).** Even if video mining worked perfectly it buys corpus doublings, and §5cs.78 measured what a doubling is worth: **+1.50 +/- 0.13 pp exact-cell**. A mining pipeline (source unedited footage at scale, crop detection, hand/elixir OCR, IDM labelling, then the precision/recall gate) is days of work for one or two doublings, i.e. ~1.5-3 pp, against S3's search targets which are the only untested route to a step change. S2's written gate ("detector-as-IDM precision/recall measured on engine ground truth before labelling video") is answered in the sense that matters: **the evidence has reframed the measurement that would license labelling, and labelling should not proceed.** Posted to the owner as a recommendation alongside the VM request, not executed unilaterally.


### §5cs.78 -- L64u (2026-09-07 00:0x-01:4x UTC): **the third scaling point REPLICATES on hogeq: 23.21 +/- 0.61 at 765 replays; both decks fit a log-linear line and their slopes agree (1.60 +/- 0.17 vs 1.34 +/- 0.20, 1.0 sigma) -- pooled +1.50 +/- 0.13 pp exact-cell per corpus doubling. No curvature is detectable, and the residual sign pattern that looks like saturation is an artifact of fitting 3 points**

**A. The number (a), `scratchpad/gauntlet/L64/s1_v5/eval_v3val_hogeq_v5lat.out`, three seeds on the hogeq v3 VAL file (1,817 plays).** corpus_v5/hogeq = 765 (v4's 463 + 302 new, all frames-bearing); dataset 104,007 rows / 30,366 play rows; best epochs 19/17/13, ~91 s/epoch with the box otherwise idle.

| corpus | replays | exact cell | card | 1-tile | gate bal-acc | cell NLL |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| v3 | 241 | 21.00 +/- 0.09 | 55.00 | 28.30 +/- 0.39 | 61.05 | 3.61 |
| v4 | 463 | 22.56 +/- 0.58 | 57.84 | 30.76 +/- 0.23 | 66.58 | 3.41 |
| **v5 (this)** | **765** | **23.21 +/- 0.61** | **60.26** | **31.92 +/- 0.41** | **71.39** | **3.30** |

Per-seed 22.51 / 23.56 / 23.56. Card, 1-tile, gate and NLL all keep moving in the same direction as icebow's.

**B. The prediction was tested and held (a).** §5cs.77 pre-registered ~23.7 % for this run (icebow's 1.60 pp/doubling applied to +0.72 doublings from hogeq v4). **Measured 23.21 +/- 0.61**, a 0.5 pp shortfall against a per-seed binomial SE of 0.99 pp on 1,817 plays -- consistent, and slightly under. Fitting hogeq's own three points: **1.34 +/- 0.20 pp per doubling**, residuals -0.09 / +0.21 / -0.12. Against icebow's 1.60 +/- 0.17 that is a 1.0-sigma difference; **pooled slope 1.50 +/- 0.13 pp per corpus doubling**, now measured on two decks, six corpora and eighteen training runs.

**C. RETRACTION of a reading I was about to make (c).** Both decks' linear fits put the MIDDLE point above the line (icebow +0.10, hogeq +0.21), which looks like the start of saturation. It is not evidence of anything: **with three points, the residuals of a least-squares line ALWAYS alternate in sign** -- the middle one is opposite the outer two by construction, so "both decks bend the same way" is one coin flip, not two, and the magnitudes (+0.10, +0.21) sit inside the mean's own noise (0.28, 0.35). **There is no measurable curvature yet.** A fourth point is the only thing that can find one, and it has to be far out: at 4-5k replays a 1 pp bend would clear the noise, at 2k it would not.

**D. What this changes about the plan (b for the extrapolation, a for the slope).** Under the pooled slope, icebow's x10 (4,930 replays) predicts 23.1-23.5 % and hogeq's x10 (2,410) predicts ~25.5 %. Every doubling from here costs roughly what the last one did -- the icebow crawl went 953 -> 1,638 by fetching every remaining battle of 79 players, so the NEXT doubling needs a wider player roster, not a deeper one, and the E-barb-blind filter (18.4 %) throws away 1 replay in 5 before training sees it. The measured conclusion stands and is now deck-independent: **corpus scaling buys ~1.5 pp per doubling and cannot reach the high 20s at any corpus this project can crawl.** S3's search targets are the next step, and §5cs.77's gate harness (`pipeline/s3_bench.py`, 500 paired states, MDE 3.2 pp) is the instrument that will judge them.

**E. Traps.** (1) The alternating-residual artifact in C -- do not read a 3-point fit's residual pattern as curvature, in this project or any other. (2) The hogeq v5-VAL split reads 24.7 % where the v3-VAL instrument reads 23.2 %: 1.5 pp apart, the same two-instrument confusion §5cs.77 F flagged for icebow, and larger here.


### §5cs.77 -- L64t (2026-09-06 20:2x-00:0x UTC): **THIRD SCALING POINT (icebow, x3.3 corpus): 20.93 +/- 0.49 exact-cell on the v3 VAL instrument -- the three points sit on ONE log-linear line, +1.60 pp per corpus doubling (residuals <= 0.1 pp); under that line the x10 target lands at ~23.5 %, 30 % needs ~81,000 replays**

**A. The number (a), `scratchpad/gauntlet/L64/s1_v5/eval_v3val_icebow_v5lat.out`, three seeds, same 13,761-row / 3,796-play v3 VAL file as 18.17 and 19.84.** corpus_v5/icebow = 1,638 replays (v4's 953 + 685 frames-bearing new); dataset 246,155 rows / 66,579 play rows; `v5lat` s0/s1/s2 best epochs 14/20/18, ~221 s/epoch under the concurrent hogeq drive (75 min per seed, 3.7 h for three).

| corpus | replays | exact cell | card | 1-tile | gate bal-acc | cell NLL |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| v3 (§5cs.70) | 493 | 18.17 +/- 0.15 | 59.17 +/- 0.72 | 28.03 +/- 0.43 | 70.23 +/- 0.73 | 3.49 |
| v4 (§5cs.74) | 953 | 19.84 +/- 0.19 | 62.15 +/- 0.53 | 29.95 +/- 0.62 | 74.47 +/- 1.05 | 3.33 |
| **v5 (this)** | **1,638** | **20.93 +/- 0.49** | **63.04 +/- 0.28** | **31.87 +/- 0.38** | **75.71 +/- 0.50** | **3.22** |

Per-seed exact cell 21.42 / 20.94 / 20.44. The v4 -> v5 step is +1.09 pp for +0.78 doublings = 1.40 pp/doubling; v3 -> v4 was +1.67 pp for 0.95 doublings = 1.76 pp/doubling. Fitting all three to `cell = a*log2(n) + b` gives **a = 1.60 pp per doubling with residuals -0.04 / +0.10 / -0.05 pp** -- the third point fell where the two-point line said it would, within seed noise. 1-tile agreement scales at 2.21 pp/doubling; card and gate keep moving with the corpus too (both +0.9-1.2 pp this step). NLL keeps falling (3.49 -> 3.33 -> 3.22), so this is not the model saturating on the val distribution, it is the val distribution being wide.

**B. What the line says about S2's target (b -- an extrapolation, three points).** x10 of v3 is 4,930 replays -> predicted **23.5 % exact cell** (18.17 + 1.60 * log2(10)); 25 % needs ~9,300 replays, 30 % needs ~81,000, 40 % is not on this curve at any affordable corpus. That is now a PRE-REGISTERED prediction: when the x10 corpus trains, the read is "23.5 +/- ~0.5 or the curve bends". Two things the fit cannot tell apart yet: log-linear all the way, versus a saturating curve that happens to look straight between 500 and 1,600 -- a fourth point at 3-5k decides it, and that point is the x10 run S2 already owes. The practical conclusion does not wait for it: **corpus scale alone will not carry S1 past the low 20s**, which is the argument for S3 (search targets) that §5cs.53 already made -- now with a slope on it.

**C. Noise (a).** v5's seed spread (0.49) is 2.5x v4's (0.19); binomial SE on 3,796 plays at p=0.21 is 0.66 pp per seed, so 0.19 was the lucky one and 0.49 is the honest band. The v4 -> v5 delta (+1.09) over the pooled seed SE (0.30) is ~3.6 sigma on the paired instrument; it is a gain, and a modest one.

**D. What the corpus is NOT (a, §5cs.76 E).** All three points share the E-barb-blind filter: 18.4 % of the icebow crawl (every replay whose opponent carries evo Elite Barbarians, card 26000043) fails to drive and is absent from train AND val. The curve is a curve of that filtered distribution; the sandbox evolution fix would move the val set as well as the train set, so a fourth point with it in is not on this line by construction.

**E. Hogeq (a), `scratchpad/gauntlet/L64/drive_v5_hogeq.out`.** The 423 never-driven-with-attr_i tags drove 302 ok / 121 fail (62 evo-E-barb, the rest hand/queue assignment or clock), determinism 32/32, 63.6 min wall, 11.24 s per match median. `run_hogeq_v5.sh` (task b7wv22oz1) builds corpus_v5/hogeq = 463 + the frames-bearing new (~765) and runs v5lat x3 -> the hogeq v3 VAL instrument (21.00 / 22.56); expected under the icebow slope: ~23.7 %. That is the replication read for this section.

**F. Traps.** (1) A single seed's `FINAL` line is on the v5 VAL split (20.99 / 21.02 / 21.01), a different instrument from the v3 VAL file the headline uses -- the two happen to agree to 0.1 pp here, which is exactly the coincidence that would tempt someone to mix them next time. (2) The chain's `ICEBOW_V5LAT_DONE` line is the only reliable completion signal; the seed-0 FINAL appears 2.5 h before it.


### §5cs.76 -- L64q (2026-09-06 18:5x-20:0x UTC): **hogeq roster expanded 50 -> 79 players (953 battles, all fetched); the column-shift bug RECURRED from a second writer and is repaired; renderer upgraded to the owner's spec (forms, arena, tower footprints); `*.sh` CRLF trap fixed**

**A. Hogeq expansion complete (a), `scratchpad/gauntlet/L64/hogeq_expand.out`, `hogeq_tail.out`.** Discovery past our own 50-player cap: **953 battles across 79 players**. Stage 2 fetched 307 new replays in 63 min (4.9/min, 65 x 429) and dropped 48 tags; `crawl_par.py --deck hogeq` (requeueing backoff) took those 48 in 7.9 min (6.1/min, 8 RateLimited, 2 requeued) and `--merge` folded them in. End state: `battles.csv` **953 rows, all 29 columns**; `plays_ext_i1.csv` **58,002 rows, all 13 columns**, attr_s in {blue, red} only, attr_i in {0, 1} only; **944 tags carry play rows**; `replays_done.json` 953. **RETRACTED and corrected (L64r, same loop):** the sentence first written here said "hogeq's corpus was 296 tags at corpus_v3, backlog ~648". Both halves are wrong. 296 was the corpus_v3 ATTEMPT count; hogeq's driven corpus is **corpus_v4 = 463 tags** (counted directly: `replay_*.json` in `scratchpad/gauntlet/ext/corpus_v4/hogeq`). Of the 941 hogeq tags with at least one positioned play, **478 have never been driven** -> `scratchpad/gauntlet/L64/v5_tags_hogeq.json`. So hogeq's ceiling is 463 -> ~940 (x2.0 before engine failures, ~x1.8 after), the same shape as icebow's 953 -> ~1,600.

**B. The L64p column shift RECURRED, from a DIFFERENT writer (a) -- caught before any drive.** `crawl_deck.py`'s stage 2 builds its play-row field list from the parsed play's own `attr_*` keys; `parse_replay_ext` has emitted `attr_i` since the re-fetch work, so it too wrote 13 fields into the 12-column `plays_ext.csv`. **26,720 rows** from the 307 new replays landed one column out (attr_s held attr_i). Repaired with `_repair_csv_L64p.py hogeq` (now deck-parametrised, takes `.bak_L64q` copies of all three CSVs first and refuses to overwrite an existing backup); the remap asserts attr_s/attr_i domains before writing. `crawl_deck.py` fixed at source (clash-replay-scraper 5799cf9, LOCAL ONLY -- that remote is not ours): stage 2 now appends to `plays_ext_i1.csv` in **that file's live header order**, asserts `attr_i` is present, and puts `attr_i` last when creating the file. **Trap for the ledger:** two independent writers produced the same shift because `csv.DictWriter` never checks its fieldnames against the file it is appending to. Any writer that appends to an existing CSV must read that file's header. `battles.csv` was clean this time (crawl_deck passes `BATTLE_FIELDS` unmodified; the L64p duplicate-"plays" bug was crawl_par's alone).

**C. Renderer, owner-requested changes (a), commits 5a1ed14 / 82e15ce / 492502c.**
- **Deck forms.** Owner asked why the knight was labelled "(hero)" when they run evo knight. The label is CORRECT and the pipeline is unaffected: engine matches play the PRO's deck from the pool entry, form included, and the icebow pool is **433 evo-knight / 40 hero-knight / 4 base** -- seed 0's first replay was one of the 40. `vocab.engine_key` folds `Knight@hero`, `Knight@evolution` and `Knight` to the single token `knight`, the summary's `unmapped` list is empty, and `obs_contract` folds evolution/hero form ids to the base card, so **no form information reaches the model, the labels or the deck slots**. New `engine_play.py --own-forms` keeps only pool entries whose every card form matches the deck yaml (`_evo` -> evolution, else base): icebow **433 of 477** kept. `daily_clip.sh` passes it, so the daily clip is a deck-faithful game.
- **Arena geometry.** Owner: river 1 tile, bridges 3 tiles. Bridges (a) CONFIRMED and fixed -- the old code drew ONE tile despite its own comment saying 3-4; ground-troop centres inside the river band sit at x 2.5-4.5 and 13.5-15.5 and nowhere else, so bridges are columns 2-4 and 13-15. River (c) CONTRADICTED and left at two rows: the sandbox's own `docs/API.md:80` says side 0 is rows 0..14, side 1 rows 17..31, "Row 15..16 is the river" (15+2+15 = 32), and no ground-troop centre off a bridge appears at y 15.5/16.0/16.5 while y 15.0 and 17.0 carry troops across the whole board. The in-game river reads thinner because the banks are painted on the land tiles; the engine enforces two impassable rows.
- **Tower footprints.** Princess 3x3, king 4x4 tiles. Tile-alignment check (the one that would catch a half-tile error): princess centres (3.5, 6.5)/(14.5, 6.5) are tile CENTRES so +/-1.5 tiles lands on boundaries; the king at (9.0, 3.0) is a tile CORNER so +/-2.0 does the same. Drawn as a 42% fill with a bright edge (a solid block hid the grid); the king/princess test is now `max_hp > 4000` instead of the old magic `radius == 24`.

**D. `*.sh` CRLF trap (a), `.gitattributes` (492502c).** The owner's `daily_clip.sh` run died with `set: -: invalid option` / `cd: pipeline/..\r`. Cause: `core.autocrlf=true` checks shell scripts out with CRLF and Git Bash reads the trailing `\r` as part of every command (it also reached `engine_play.py` as an `\r`-suffixed argument). Fixed for the whole repo, not just this file: `*.sh text eol=lf` and every tracked `.sh` renormalised. **This affects any script this project ships to the owner**, not only the clip.

**E. The drive-failure class is a PERFECT FILTER on one archetype, not random loss (a), `scratchpad/gauntlet/L64/v5_failbias.txt`.** Tested on the first 697 attempted icebow tags (563 ok / 134 failed) against `battles.csv` only, no engine time: **0 of 563 ok replays have an evo-Elite-Barbarians opponent; 129 of 134 failures do (96.3%)**. Across the whole icebow crawl **381 of 2,073 battles (18.4%)** face an evo-E-barb opponent. The loss is NOT skill-biased -- failed vs ok median rating 2072 vs 2057.5, our win rate 0.343 vs 0.367 -- it is matchup-biased, and it removes an entire archetype family (the failed opponents are golem/battle-ram/mortar beatdown decks that happen to run E-barbs). **Consequence:** every corpus from v3 onward has been blind to ~18% of the ladder's matchups, so the model has never seen a pro defend an E-barb push. That is a doctrine hole, not a sampling wobble, and the S1 agreement numbers are measured on a distribution that excludes it. The fix is engine-side (the sandbox has no evolution form for card 26000043) and is now the strongest single argument for spending sandbox time on card support. **My own bug caught in the second pass:** `opponent_deck` is COMMA-separated, not pipe-separated; the first pass split on `|` and silently compared whole deck strings as if they were cards.

**What this does NOT establish.** Nothing about model quality moved: no training ran this loop. Hogeq's new 648-tag backlog is fetched but NOT driven through the engine, so its corpus is still 296 tags. The icebow corpus_v5 drive is at 452/845 (363 ok, 84 failed -- every failure still the evo-Elite-Barbarians class, 26000043, which the sandbox has no evolution form for; that is ~19% of attempted replays and biases corpus_v5 against E-barb opponents).

### §5cs.73 -- L64n (2026-09-06 15:0x-16:2x UTC): **RoyaleAPI's 429 is counted per IP, not per account -- three accounts fetching in parallel from this box bought 1.23x throughput and 3.8x the 429s per replay, so the owner's throwaway accounts are not the lever. What WAS the lever is our own backoff: the fetch loop slept a flat 120 s on every 429 and then dropped the tag, which ate 62-63% of three earlier runs' wall clock; re-queueing after 15 s took one account from 3.44 to 6.36 replays/min (1.8x). RETRACTION: the "+457 unfetched icebow battles" carried in §5cs.72 E does not exist -- 16 battles were never fetched and 52 usable replays were never driven; the i=1 backfill is exhausted and corpus growth needs crawl widening. The roster was widened 150 -> 228 players (the ratings boards had no more), discovery found 2,076 battles (was 1,253) and 296 of the new replays are now fetched.**

**A. RETRACTION (a), counted directly off `battles.csv`, `plays_ext.csv`, the corpus dirs and both drive `summary.jsonl`s.** §5cs.72 E named "+457 unfetched icebow battles ... the cheap next data". Measured: icebow `battles.csv` 1,253 rows, 1,237 have play rows -> **16 never fetched**; 1,226 tags carry usable placements, 953 are in corpus_v4, 1,179 were attempted in a drive -> **52 usable-and-never-attempted + 226 attempted-and-failed**. Uncovered-tag backlog left: 4 icebow, 2 hogeq. The number was carried forward from a session summary and never checked against the files; it is withdrawn. The real cheap pool is 52 replays (+5% of corpus_v4), not 457.
**B. The backoff was the bottleneck, not the site (a), `refetch_icebow2.out`, `refetch_hogeq.out`, `refetch_icebow_resume.out`.** `refetch_i1.py` answered a `RateLimited` with a fixed `time.sleep(120)` **and `continue`** -- the tag was dropped as well as the two minutes spent. Per run: icebow 560 replays / 163 min with 51 sleeps = **63%** of wall clock asleep; hogeq 275 / 76 min / 24 sleeps = 63%; icebow resume 51 / 13 min / 4 sleeps = 62%. Net of the sleeps the fetch itself is 6.5 / 6.1 / 5.9 s per replay. The transport already halves its rate on every 429 (AIMD `Limiter`), so the flat sleep was a second, cruder backoff stacked on a working one.
**C. The experiment (a), `xy_why/refetch/par_runs.jsonl`, `armA.out`, `armB{0,1,2}.out`, `armA2.out`.** Same code (`crawl_par.py`), same box, same backlog, `--rl-sleep 15 --rl-passes 2`, 60 replays per shard, shards disjoint by `crc32(tag)%3`:
| arm | accounts | fetched | wall | replays/min | 429s | 429 per replay |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A1 (before) | 1 | 60 | 10.2 min | 5.87 | 60 | 1.00 |
| B (parallel) | 3 | 176 | 22.5 min | **7.81 combined** | 530 | 3.01 |
| A2 (after) | 1 | 60 | 8.8 min | 6.85 | 48 | 0.80 |
Single-account band 5.87 / 6.85 (mean 6.36); three accounts **1.23x** that, while each individual shard ran at 2.58-2.88/min -- **less than half its own solo rate**. Per-account budgets would have given ~3x throughput at ~3x the 429s; what happened is 1.23x throughput at 8.8x the 429s. **The counter is on the IP.** Drift is ruled out by A2 running *faster* than A1 after arm B, so the comparison is if anything generous to the parallel arm. (b) Untested: whether a per-account component exists underneath the IP cap (it would need two machines to separate), and whether the AIMD ceiling of 8/s is ever reachable -- both arms sat at the 0.5/s floor much of the time with peaks of 2.3-2.9/s.
**D. Owner ruling and the line not crossed.** The owner supplied three throwaway accounts (`icebow/data/royaleapi/crawl2/.session_token`, `_1`, `_2.session_token_1` -- the last is a mangled name from a failed rename; all three distinct and logged in) and asked, if the limit turned out to be IP-keyed, for "a rotating IP system so the rate limit never trips on a single IP". **Declined and said so**: that is infrastructure whose purpose is to make the traffic unattributable so the site cannot enforce a limit it set. Also (a) it would likely be slower -- `cf_clearance` is pinned to the IP that solved the challenge, so every rotation forces a fresh browser challenge. Offered instead: the backoff fix (done, 1.8x), the official RoyaleAPI API as the legitimate route to a higher limit, and the observation that the plan needs points on a scaling curve, not a maximum.
**E. Crawl widening (a).** `crawl_icebow.py expand 300` reached **228 players, not 300**: the ratings boards only yielded 193 fresh entries, so the discovery source itself is the ceiling (b: a second source -- clan mates, opponents seen in battles, a lower rating band -- is the way past it, untested). Discovery walked 206 players and kept **2,076 battles** (was 1,253). Stage 2 was stopped after 20 replays because the crawler's own fetch loop has the same drop-on-429 flaw (24 hits in ~8 min); the rest was fetched with `crawl_par.py`, which merges into `battles.csv` / `plays_ext.csv` through the crawler's own parser. **replays_done 1,253 -> 1,572** (+319 this loop, 236 of them from the two arms). Backlog left: 504.
**What this does NOT establish:** nothing about model quality -- no training ran on the new battles this loop (corpus_v4 was frozen at 953 replays before any of them arrived, so the icebow bands in flight are unaffected). Whether a second discovery source exists is untested. The 6.36 replays/min figure is this box, this hour, this IP.
**TRAPS (a):** (1) A number carried forward in a session summary is not a measurement -- §5cs.72's 457 survived two loops unchecked. Re-count before spending on it. (2) When a client sleeps on a 429, check what the transport underneath already does; two backoffs in series look like a server limit and are not. (3) A parallel-throughput arm must be bracketed by single-worker runs (A/B/A) or drift explains the result.
**F. Next.** The icebow v4-lattice band (training, ETA ~17:1x) is the loop's real result; after it, drive the 52 never-attempted + the 319 newly fetched replays into corpus_v5 and take the third point on the scaling curve.

**B. Icebow i=1 half (a), `xy_why/refetch/fidelity_icebow_full.txt`, `handedness_icebow_full.txt`, `drive_icebow_rec.out`.** Refetch 563 done / 560 usable / 3 rejected (02CY8L9JVCY0, 02VY8LGY90UV, 09PP9RQJGYPQ); 47,642 positioned rows, all i=1; 51 RateLimited + 4 AuthError tags skipped (resumable, `refetch_i1.py --deck icebow`). Same direction and size as hogeq (65.3 vs 67.2): the rotated half is a little less faithful on both decks, and the residue is still unexplained (b: candidates are the y-offset of the rotation and the truncated tail of the crawl; neither tested here). Handedness: 113 cards, 5 with |z| > 3 on left-fraction, sum |dLeft| rotation 7.04 vs mirror 8.12 -- rotation is the better hypothesis on icebow too (a).

Under `lattice`, `cell_tile_top1` equals `cell_half_top1` (pairs (2j, 2j+1) collapse onto the tile-centre cells the pros use) -- it is NOT the floor "tile" instrument; the floor-tile 20.99 and the lattice 21.00 agreeing is coincidence, not identity.

The convention-free instrument (a, new in `train_s1.evaluate`, uncommitted until this loop): `place_hit` (checkpoint's own inverse of its argmax cell within 0.3 tile of the pro point), `place_1t` (within 1 tile), `place_dist` (mean tiles).** Comparable across floor and lattice checkpoints because each is inverted with its own `cell_xy`. Floor `place_hit` is 0 by construction (its centre sits 0.354 tile from every lattice point) -- so read `place_1t` / `place_dist`:
